To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
unanticipated government spending has negative effects on economic growth, and that these effects are stronger for industrial economies than for emerging economies.

(i) the effects of unexpected government expenditures on GDP growth are negative and significant, with higher effects for developed economies; and (ii) the effects of anticipated government expenditures on GDP are negative, but smaller, and significant.
unanticipated government spending has a negative impact on output growth, and this impact is higher for developed economies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the effects of fiscal policy depend on whether government expenditures are expected or unanticipated.
the effects of fiscal policy on growth and how these effects differ between developed and developing countries.
the role of government expenditures in the growth process, and how this role is affected by expectations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the negative effect of government expenditures on output growth is not a myth.
the effects of government expenditures on output growth are negative and larger than those of the standard Solow model.
unanticipated government expenditure has a negative impact on economic growth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effects of government expenditures on economic growth are not always positive, and that the effects of unexpected fiscal policy shocks are more negative for output growth than anticipated fiscal policy shocks.
the effects of government expenditures on growth depend on their expected and unexpected components.
unexpected government expenditures are contractionary in the long-run.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fiscal policy is not a neutral policy tool.
the impact of unanticipated government expenditures on output growth is larger in more developed economies, which may be due to their more efficient financial markets.
, when it comes to output effects, the timing of government expenditures matters.
